en: You stirred up countless feuds and quarrels.
Whenever you wished, in this land—
Where is the blessed night, the night of joy?
Yesterday, when bored, we hunted roe deer;
When not bored, the dear people
Romped and played freely.
Where are the days we had before?
Ruling the people and keeping the nation,
You have become sultan of the Argyn.
Shattering all these people to pieces,
You have sucked them dry like a black leech.
You brought slaughter and seized the frontier,
You destroyed all and lit a fire within,
You sharpened your spear to excess,
You began your wicked frenzy.
Bent old folk and young children
You left without descendants.
You swaggering madman,
Your sin will fall upon yourself,
Your guilt upon your black-crowned head.
Can one prosper by harboring a traitor?
Wild in thought and foul at heart,
Strange in tidings and mighty in venom—
Can Kanchoro truly be a brother?
Would a son of man tend as a brother
A boar that gores from among the herd,
Or call a dragon his kin?
Without taking revenge on that burning wretch,
Dear brother-in-law who made him your guardian,
Can your deed be pleasing to God?
At heart he is our enemy;
In the end, the conflict will multiply,
Son, have you forgotten this?
When they buried you beneath a haystack,
Cut open your shoulder and gouged it,
Enslaved your heroic soul,
And made you gather firewood
For forty hardened herdsmen,
It was Kanchoro who inflicted that disgrace,
And valiant Kyyaz who seized your hands;
It was he who gave the command,
A foe more sinister than any mortal.
Will you not repay the slaughter
And humiliation, Külchoro?
Will you not offer the madman
As a sacrifice, Külchoro?
Let such a traitor disappear,
And let your affairs become clear as glass!
From rocky, cliff-bound Keng-Kol,
We have come to recover our people;
From the pig swollen with wrath,
We have come to take revenge.
From the scattered, ruined Kyrgyz,
We have come to gather counsel;
From the dragon-shaped pig,
We have come to exact vengeance!
The finest among us are our khans;
Drinking red blood and swallowing dust,
Let us all perish together.
Let us snap in a row like threads of hair,
Our precious lives we would not spare.
Let our blood flow like water;
How can our souls find rest
If we swallow grief without revenge?
How can our souls find rest
Without fighting and drinking blood?
The past disgrace and great calamity—
If you are a man, Külchoro,
Take them to heart.
God the Creator made humankind;
If every soul were weak,
All would wander aimlessly.
In the remote tract where no horse could travel,
Upon you and my noble uncle
They drew their bows like pouring rain,
And shot arrows like falling hail.
Stirring total turmoil and strife,
They drove the people into terror,
Seized the land where the nation made its living,
Passed the heights and took the mountain belt.
Desiring wicked turmoil,
Your two uncles Chynkojo and Toltoy—
Claiming, “Those two uncles slaughtered them,”
They incited valiant Kyyaz.
They camped along the Kök-Ötök,
And reveled together with Kyyaz.
Their blood-grooved iron-shafted spears
They gripped short and brandished,
And without sparing a single one of you,
They unleashed a massacre.
They drenched their spears in blood,
And every precious, worthy life
They felled and laid upon the earth.
Blood-red calamity Kanchoro
Planted his steel against the ground,
And never once regarded
The kinship of distant relatives.
With their matchcords glowing red,
Shayymbet and Baytaylak
Destroyed all the khans’ sons,
Those fire-scorched swine.
They pierced them through and took the khans,
And took the lives of those who deemed themselves mighty;
Red gold and blue silver,
And countless herds they seized as plunder.
Climbing a hill, he shouted,
And summoned an army of ten thousand.
In long boots and leather trousers,
With a pacing mare and crimson sheath,
Slave Joydur urged them onward,
Craving ever greater turmoil;
When he spread sorrow far and wide,
It was his own doing.
What manner of man was Kanchoro,
Who fired arrows at his own kin!
The wrathful Chürök began,
And she and Kanykey flared with rage;
With the fluttering life within her breast,
The furious woman launched
A great and dreadful conflict.
That leopardess, your mother Kanykey,
Who knew custom and governed the people,
When in the palace built at Talas
She became mother to the whole world,
There was no person as mighty as she.
Your precious, fierce mother
Would leave no necessary deed undone.
Her dear kinsman Bölökbay—
For the master smith Bölökbay himself,
For the black eyes of the smith David,
She poured spirits and offered butter,
Serving him and submitting,
Pleading with the smith David.
She had racehorses tethered to the line,
Six thousand gelded camels and eighty breeding camels—
All these she had given
As payment to master Bölökbay.
“Make it like Jangkol’s,” she said,
Pouring out her wealth in supplication;
“My dear kinsman,” she cried, wringing her hands,
And pleaded with Bölökbay.
He understood her service;
The noble master smith Bölökbay
Obeyed Kanykey.
“My child, dear kinswoman, I shall agree;
From generation to generation,
Your descendants shall carry it as a gift,
And smile whenever they behold it.
They shall value and understand
The worth of the object made by David;
When it strikes a grief-stricken, aching heart,
It shall split it into two.
Can this wrathful pig of old
Become your brother if you shelter him?
Is it right to call the roaring wretch
Your brother?
He made us slaves with blood-red backsides,
Burned multitudes and made them booty,
Showing his enmity openly;
You burned us outright and set us aflame.
He made us claw our faces bloody,
And let down our black hair in mourning;
He let the Jediger ride
Kambar-Ata’s gray stallion,
And placed the khan’s treasury and palace
Under Kanchoro’s command.
Rather than stand watching without revenge,
Rather than commit this deed,
Let us sink down, never having been born;
Death is better than life—
Better that we die!
Having blunted our blades,
And destroyed our worthy heroes,
What shall we gain by making
That brazen pig our brother?
Let us cut off this mane by the handful
And perish in the slaughter!”
So saying, Aichürök
Stiffened in fury;
Her eyes blazed with fire,
And her white teeth, gleaming like crystal,
She ground one against another.
When she hissed like a dragon,
What living soul could restrain her?
Kanchoro upon the throne
Leapt like a hunting eagle.
You should have seen your wife Chürök,
That flashing, fierce woman—
She lunged like a blue tiger.
From the hell and calamity he had inflicted,
From the cup he himself had filled,
How could Kanchoro escape?
As I prepare to leave this mortal world,
I have drawn forth my true blade.
I tested it by pinching every part,
And finding not a flaw as small as a fly,
I myself tempered it in earnest.
All my skill and remaining strength—
My child, I spent upon it.
Then he went away, weeping bitterly.
From the old man’s eyes
Dark blood poured like hail;
He screamed and wept aloud,
Kissing the hilt and sobbing.
Long ago, Bölökbay left
As an inheritance the white Tintay,
With a jeweled pommel and golden hilt,
And a golden sheath to hold it.
He twisted and tested its hilt,
Never ceasing to fear
That it might slip from the hand.
He often spoke of its noble form:
“I shall draw it against the foe I meet”—
Kanykey herself had made this vow.
When your mother escaped from slavery
And God granted her desire,
Aichürök, daughter of the peri,
Prepared to present Seytek
At the rock of Kayypchy,
As she had planned from the beginning.
The white Tintay, willingly bestowed—
“Let the children receive it as a gift,
So that upon the black-faced enemy
They may bring sudden ruin.”
The white Tintay given as a gift,
For Aichürök, champion among women,
To prepare against the wrathful khan,
Ready to spill blood;
With matchless agility,
She ran beyond all reckoning,
Bounding and gathering herself like a doe.
The white Tintay received as a gift—
May your enemy behold its fame;
May this wondrous blade become
A guardian of a precious life.
If swung with all one’s strength,
The foe it truly strikes will surely die...
Whoever feels the breath
Of its unyielding true temper will know it.
My precious kinswoman, I shall agree,
To take the son of your eldest son,
And preserve your battle cry.
When cataracts veil my darkening eyes,
When I have grown old,
My swan-white beard turned pale,
My raven eyes turned red,
My able body worn away,
My steel blunted and spent,
When I am no longer capable;
When I have eaten and drunk my fill,
And my kinswoman has given me my shroud,
When my time has come to depart;
When my breast grows cold and my eyes close,
When my time has come to depart;
When my fleeting soul leaves
This mortal world, my child;
